articles.title: Longing for a Time Before Smartphones
articles.author: Jinae West
articles.content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Gen Z has romanticized the technology of the ’90s—or the era’s lack of it. Young people long for a time when they were looking at one another instead of at their phones. But could that nostalgia for a smartphone-free society actually help guide the future?
That’s one of the driving questions in the latest season of How to Touch Grass, co-hosted by Julie Beck and Natalie Brennan. This week on Radio Atlantic, we’re sharing the first episode, with an introduction by Hanna Rosin.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Hanna Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic.
Do I remember a time before I had a smartphone? Of course I do.
[Music]
Long dinners with friends, nothing buzzing or pinging. Standing in line with nothing to do but think, and stare. Reading an entire book in two days. And then back to when I was a teenager: telling my friends that I liked or maybe didn’t like their new perm, like, in person. I guess that’s what they call nostalgia?
But nostalgia is working a little differently for Gen Z. I actually lived through the things I miss. But a lot of them long for a time when they weren’t even alive—an era of iPods and CD players and calling your friends on a landline.
[Music]
I find it strange that people in their 20s are now fixated on shows I watched when I was in my 20s, like Friends. It seems like longing that goes nowhere? But maybe nostalgia for the past, even an unfamiliar past, can help shape the future.
Today we have something special: the first episode from How to Touch Grass. It’s the latest season of The Atlantic’s How To series. It’s all about how we might renegotiate our relationships with technology and untangle ourselves from guilt and habit and mindless patterns. Step one: Go touch grass, probably.
 
 I’ll let co-hosts Julie Beck and Natalie Brennan take it from here.
[Music]
Julie Beck: If you had one word—it can be a noun, it can be an adjective, it can be any part of speech that you want—to describe your overall relationship to technology at this moment in time.
Voice memo: Antagonistic?
Voice memo: Complicated.
Voice memo: Fraught.
Voice memo: Connection.
Voice memo: I think of it as an addiction. Similar to how I relate to, like, sugar or anything else that I sort of compulsively overindulge in.
Beck: What’s your word?
Voice memo: Indentured.
Voice memo: I was gonna say reluctant, but maybe that’s not right.
Voice memo: Very frequent user.
Beck: Okay, that’s a lot of words, but we’ll take it.
Beck: I’m Julie Beck, a staff writer at The Atlantic.
Natalie Brennan: And I’m Natalie Brennan, a producer at The Atlantic.
Beck: This is How to Touch Grass.
Amy Poehler: Have you heard the young people say “touch grass”?
Tiktok user: I switched to a dumb phone. This is the Nokia 2780.
Amy Poehler: It’s like a term, basically, which is like, Get off your phones.
Subway Takes: Smartphones are evil, they’re ruining society, and we need to just stop. 100% disagree.
Amy Poehler: Get off the internet, and go outside and touch grass.
Tiktok user 2: I nominate everyone for the Touch Grass Challenge. Go outside and touch some grass like I’m doing right now. Go, go, go!
[Birds chirping]
Beck: In this season, we’ll be exploring the often-fraught, always-changing relationship people have with technology. And the ways that, in this moment, the terms of the relationship are being renegotiated.
Beck: Natalie, you could throw your phone in the East River. Why don’t you?
Brennan: It’s not really just about my phone. I wanna throw your phone in there too, Julie. But I can’t take everyone’s phone.
Beck: Mmm.
Brennan: So I think what I mean to say is that I yearn for a pre-phone era.
Beck: I think we’re not the only ones who have this fantasy. It’s all over TikTok.
TikTok user: What’s the biggest trend of 2026 gonna be? Analog. This past year, we’ve seen the rise of nostalgia; the switch from iPhone cameras to digital cameras …
TikTok user 2: Here’s how to actually be more analog in 2026. First, I wanna …
TikTok user 3: The analog era is here. And while audiences say they want to go offline, with Gen Z and millennials openly expressing their desires to break from an online world and find deeper …
TikTok user 4: I stopped using an iPhone three weeks ago and the effects have genuinely been profound. 
Beck: In the past few years, there’s been no shortage of people advocating for reducing screen time. But another force that has been inspiring people to rethink how they use their devices lately is: nostalgia.
[Music]
Clay Routledge: We can often feel overwhelmed in the moment and in the challenges we face today. It’s hard to see past them. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment.
Beck: Clay Routledge and his colleagues have been studying what’s behind this widespread yearning for a time before smartphones and before social media. Clay is a psychologist who specializes in nostalgia, and he’s also the author of Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life.
Beck: Clay, hello, welcome!
Routledge: Hi, Julie.
Beck: I see you’ve got an Atari poster behind you. There’s some kind of video game that is too small for me to see what it is. What is it?
Routledge: On the shelf, I’ve got an old Nintendo, the original NES. Then I’ve got the Robotron arcade game, which is an arcade from the ’80s, and the Atari poster. So yeah, lots of video-game nostalgia from different brands and decades.
Beck: Oh, man. Perfect. Okay. It’s a nostalgia museum at your house.
Routledge: It is indeed.
Beck: Clay, just to get started, what is the point of being nostalgic about anything?
Routledge: So nostalgia is, in psychological terms, what we call a self-regulatory resource. It helps us navigate life in important ways. We don’t know the future; it’s uncertain. And so it can also be a great source of anxiety. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment and say, You know, there’s a bigger picture. Right now, maybe I’m experiencing stress or loneliness, or I just went through some difficult challenge, but my life is full of other types of experiences, and if I had these more fulfilling experiences in the past, then I should be able to have them in the future.
Beck: Yeah, I asked you about the past, and you immediately started talking about the future. Do people tend to misunderstand nostalgia by assuming, as I did, that it’s about the past?
Routledge: So nostalgia, the dictionary definition is something like: a sentimental longing for the past. When you present it like that, then it makes sense that people would assume, well, nostalgia might even be people getting stuck in the past.
Beck: Mm-hmm.
Routledge: Or looking to the past too warmly and not, you know, dealing with their present realities head-on. Turns out that when people engage in this kind of nostalgic reflection, in a lot of ways they’re talking about their issues today, and they’re thinking about tomorrow.
So nostalgia actually has this very forward-looking, unexpected, hopeful quality. We often are looking for specific things that can help us with particular challenges and anxieties we’re facing, so—
Beck: Mmm.
Routledge: —and I’m articulating this as if this is happening at some deliberate or conscious level, ’cause I’m talking about more of the scientific study of nostalgia and what we’ve learned from that kind of empirical work. But in reality, of course, this is just happening almost unconsciously. People are often using nostalgia without even realizing it.
Beck: That makes sense to me when it comes to, you know, my own life and my own past experiences, right? But Clay, what about nostalgia for a time from before you were even alive? There was a stat from a survey you worked on that really struck me, which was you found that 60 percent of Gen Z wished that they could return to a time before everyone was, quote, “plugged in.” And the other generations said that too, but they actually lived through that time, whereas Gen Z has no actual memories of a time before the internet existed. So was that surprising to you?
Routledge: It was. When we first found that, I was pretty surprised because most of the work, the research on nostalgia, including the research I’ve done, is focused on autobiographical—
Beck: Mm.
Routledge: —memory, but to your point, what we started to discover with that survey is: People actually have a longing for the past that predates them. Now, of course, if you’ve studied art and culture more abstractly, we’ve long known that people have favorite eras that they’re interested in, whether it’s the architecture or the music or the fashion. So we’ve known there’s this aesthetic nostalgia that’s historical—
Beck: Mm-hmm.
Routledge: —but what we were surprised to find is that young adults have so much to look forward to in the future, and we typically think of youth as very future-oriented, but the majority of them were saying that they longed for a time really before modern technology, but really before they were alive.
And then since that survey, we’ve just done more and more surveys finding that around two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they’re nostalgic for a time before they were alive.
Beck: Right. So this seems like a little bit more than just a like, We’re bringing low-rise jeans back, right?—
Routledge: (Laughs.) Yeah.
Beck: —if they’re saying they would like to live in the past. I mean, how common is it for generations to yearn that way for a past they never actually knew, or is something about this unique?
Routledge: Yeah. There’s not a lot of research or really any research in previous generations when they were the same age as Gen Z. But we do know from our own work, in general, people tend to become nostalgic when they’re going through major life transitions or disruptions, or when the world feels particularly chaotic or uncertain.
Beck: Mmm.
Routledge: Regardless of whether you’re, you know, 20 or 60, sometimes there are sources of cultural inspiration that people wanna draw from in a more shared bank of memories that aren’t just your own, but are the memories we share as a culture. And here’s the key thing, I think, and this is the case with Gen Z too. It really isn’t the case that people want to live in the past.
Beck: Okay.
Routledge: If you start asking people Would they give up all of the modern advances? they say no. What they’re saying is they have a sentiment for some aspect of the past that they think that we’re missing today. I think there is something about Gen Z in this, you know, as digital natives who grew up in this era where this major transition from the analog world to the digital world, that seems to be sparking a particularly potent type—
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: —of historical nostalgia. And then the irony is technology really is helping facilitate this. Because how are Gen Z adults learning about retro trends? They’re on TikTok, right?
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: And so it’s funny how the technology that, on the one hand, is the source of frustration and anxiety is also the vehicle through which they’re being introduced to the analog world.
Beck: Okay, so, I was wondering because, you know, when you say you wanna return to another era, an earlier era, maybe they’re not thinking about the things they would be dissatisfied with in the earlier era, right? Like—
Routledge: Right.
Beck: —lack of social progress that we have since made. It seems like you’re saying it tends to be about something particular that they are yearning for rather than, like, a holistic desire to go back to all the things.
Routledge: Yeah, absolutely. You know, one of the things I think people don’t appreciate about nostalgia, ’cause it’s often portrayed as just repeating something.
Beck: Mm.
Routledge: And it really isn’t. It’s more of, like, a revising. There’s a creative process. Humans are really a progress-oriented species. We’re never content; we’re never satisfied. We’re always tinkering. We always think things can be a little bit better, and it’s frustrating, right? Because it often means we’re not ever just really happy. But that’s also the thing that drives us to positive change, and nostalgia’s very much an ingredient of that.
[Music]
Beck: So Natalie, I can remember really distinctly the last time that I was ever truly lost.
Brennan: Mm-hmm.
Beck: It was like two months before I would get my first smartphone. The year was 2013.
Brennan: So you were—how old were you then?
Beck: I was 23.
Brennan: Okay.
Beck: I was in St. Petersburg, Russia, and what I would do to get around in the days before I had Google Maps available on my phone all the time is I would look up directions on the computer before I left, and I would write them down, sometimes on my hand.
Brennan: Totally.
Beck: I had done this: I’d gotten my directions together, I had gone sightseeing, and I was heading back to my hotel. But I was so jet-lagged that I fell asleep on the bus, and when I woke up, I had no idea if I’d already missed my stop or not.
Brennan: Oh no. Do you speak Russian?
Beck: I definitely don’t. Um, but I went up to the bus driver anyways, to try to ask him if we had already passed the stop. A lot of people spoke English, you know, but he got really angry and was like, “You can’t talk to me while I’m driving.” So he wouldn’t talk to me, and I’m freaking out. And this young woman behind me, she can see how upset I am, and she speaks English. So she comes up and tells me, like, yes, we already passed the stop for my hotel. Lovely woman. She gets off the bus with me at the next stop—
Brennan: No!
Beck: —and she drew me a map on a piece of paper that she had, and she was like, “There’s this one really long road. You just have to walk on that road the whole way back.” And the hotel was on that road, so you would see it, you know, looming in the distance. And I remember she said, “It's really far. You’re gonna think that you’re never gonna get there, but I promise if you just keep walking on this one road, you will get back to the hotel.”
Brennan: Oh my God. I’d be crying. Were you crying?
Beck: Oh, for sure.
Brennan: Yeah. (Laughs.)
Beck: So anyway, I set off down the road for a really long time. It felt like miles, multiple miles.
Brennan: You’re alone.
Beck: I’m alone. I was traveling alone. When, out of nowhere, this man comes running towards me.
Brennan: Nope.
Beck: Well, it turns out he’s from a cruise ship that is docked nearby, and he is trying to find McDonald’s.
Brennan: No.
Beck: I tell him what happened. And he says, “Oh, well that’s the same direction as my cruise ship that I need to get back to. Like, I’ll just walk with you until you get back.” Eventually, my hotel appears on the horizon, finally. And there’s really no other word for it; he, like, scampers off into the night, and as he runs away, he shouts, “Goodbye, Julie. I love you.”
Brennan: No!
Beck: So anyway, I made it home safely. And that was the last time I was ever lost in my life.
Brennan: Wow. I’m feeling both jealousy and awe, in that I will—I’ve never had that experience. I mean, I’ve been on public transportation, of course, while my phone has died.
Beck: Yeah.
Brennan: But I have never been an adult without a smartphone.
Beck: I am kind of nostalgic for that memory, because it was one of those moments that really restores your faith in humanity. You know?
Brennan: Yeah.
Beck: Like, I was screwed, and people appeared, and they helped me when I really needed it. And that made me feel, like, swaddled tightly in the fabric of human community. And none of that would’ve happened if I had a smartphone, if I had Google Maps.
Brennan: Yeah. I’ve only really ever had that experience manufactured for me.
Beck: Really?
Brennan: Yes. I went on this program in college. It was called the New England Literature Program.
Beck: Okay.
Brennan: And it’s basically living in cabins on a lake in New Hampshire for six weeks. And when you arrive, they take your phone for the remainder of the program. There’s no personal technology, no phones, no computers.
Beck: Hmm.
Brennan: You read Emerson, Thoreau.
Beck: Of course you do. Who else would you read?
Brennan: You visit Walden Pond. (Laughs.) And on the second day of the program is Get Lost Day.
Beck: Okay.
Brennan: In the morning, we learned how to use a compass, and then, promptly, were blindfolded, which now sounds like a cult, but it wasn’t—
Beck: (Laughs.)
Brennan: —to different locations, in groups, and then shown on a map where we were and where camp was, and told to get back by dinner.
Beck: Wait, wait, wait. Where—like, describe to me the vibe of, like, where—
Brennan: We were dropped off? Field.
Beck: Field. End of sentence?
Brennan: Yep.
Beck: Field. Okay, okay, okay.
Brennan: In the beginning, you’re quite confident that you’re on track, and I think a few hours in, it became quite clear to us that we weren’t making it back to camp, and that we would just find a ride later in the day. We would ask somebody to take us back to camp, and just kind of spent the day enjoying and exploring.
Beck: Oh, wow. So you just pivoted. You were like, This is never happening. We’re not gonna find our way back.
Brennan: No.
Beck: Let's just be in this field.
Brennan: We’re gonna—we are going to touch grass and vibe.
Beck: Okay.
Brennan: I’m sure we were walking for hours, but I think the bigger point, instead, was to, like, get to know each other. You’re placed into vulnerability. You’re going to share this experience. But I do think extremely fondly about the program. Those whole six weeks really just sparkle with nostalgia for me, and I really struggle to differentiate between how much of that experience was the “no tech” of it all—
Beck: Hmm
Brennan: —and how much of it was just the experience at large.
[Music]
Beck: Clay, what do you think the thing is that people who are nostalgic for the ’90s or the 2000s are wanting to bring forward and revise, as you say?
Routledge: If I could sum it up using two words.
Beck: That’d be great.
Routledge: I would say control and community.
Beck: Mm.
Routledge: And the reason I’m picking those two words is because we’ve done, in addition to the surveys, we’ve done a number of qualitative projects that, you know, look at the types of nostalgic-related posts that Gen Z adults make on different social media and websites that they frequent. And what you often find is this sense that they love technology, but they wanna be in control of it, not feel controlled by it.
Beck: Mm-hmm.
Routledge: So it’s that more sense of intentional use, and this is why I think you see these interesting trends like Gen Z buying old iPods and, you know, they wanna have their new iPhone. Everybody wants to have the Uber app and all the different things that make our lives a little more convenient, but sometimes there’s a sense of like, Maybe there’s a more low-tech option that allows me just to listen to music.
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: And the community. I think Gen Z’s figuring out that there’s something missing in computer-mediated social relationships. And on the one hand, the social media’s really useful ’cause it helps you organize events, meet people you would’ve never met. But at the same time, they look at this time period right before smartphones really became dominant, and they said, Oh, there’s a sense of freedom. There’s a sense of organic social life, and—
Beck: You’re not looking at your phone the whole time.
Routledge: —mm hmm. And they want to build that in. A lot of times, nostalgia’s framed in a very zero-sum sort of framework, where it’s like: You’re either for the past or you’re for the future.
And I think what Gen Z’s showing us is they want both. And there’s something to say intergenerationally about this, which is maybe young people are learning about ’90s fashions on TikTok, but then what we often find is that sparks a conversation with older generations, whether it’s a parent or a coworker you know, or somebody in their run club, that they’re like, Oh, was life really like this? Did you really do this? And it creates a dialogue between generations, which I think, in this era of where everyone has their own screens and their own tailored content, is something that people feel like they’re really missing.
Beck: Yeah. I remember my dad always used to talk about that—that sort of, like, shared experience of music, ’cause you had to, like, put on a record, and so everybody’s listening to the Rolling Stones whether they like it or not. And now, obviously, we just have our sort of, like, isolated pods, and you don’t know that I’m listening to that same Taylor Swift song like 10 times in a row, and you’ll never know.
Routledge: (Laughs.) Now I know.
Beck: Okay. Yeah, I did—yeah, now everybody knows.
[Music]
Beck: We’re gonna take a quick break. When we come back: Why is this analog nostalgia bubbling up now? Do you think it has anything to do with AI coming on the scene?
[Break]
Beck: Clay, why do you think nostalgia for analog technology is so popular right now? Does the buzz about AI have anything to do with it?
Routledge: I think AI is part of it, because if machines can do all this cognitive work, and maybe even creative work, that we thought was the distinct domain of humanity, now you’re seeing more of this holistic thinking of like, what is the essence of being a person?
Beck: Mm-hmm.
Routledge: And this nostalgia, I think, is really helping people get that sense of embodiment, of like, this isn’t just cognition. There’s something about emotion, spirituality, living in the world, having these tactile sensory experiences, in-person, real contact with other real human beings.
Beck: Just with like, all the parts of life that are more than just being a brain in a jar, basically?
Routledge: Yeah, that’s a great way of putting it. And if you look at a lot of the consumer nostalgic trends, many of them driven by Gen Z, they’re very much that, right?
They’re the rise of independent bookstores, the growth of music festivals, book clubs, game nights, old tech, technology that’s not online that you have to—I was talking to somebody the other day about retro video games, and they were saying, “Well, one thing that’s really cool is you have to sit next to each other to play, like two players.”
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: You’re not playing online. And so I think there’s this idea that even if it’s technology, even if it’s like video games or music, you mentioned vinyl records, which, you know, one of the big drivers of vinyl-record sales is Gen Z. They’re these low-tech, retro-tech trends that really seem to be about being out in the world, handling things, engaging with people. That’s a big driver of this.
[Music]
Beck: Natalie, let’s play a little game where I name a thing that people might be nostalgic for, and then try to psychoanalyze what it means about what they actually want from their relationship to technology.
Brennan: Okay.
Beck: Okay, my first one: I see a lot of memes about people missing the days when people had computer rooms in their home. Like, picture a big wooden entertainment center with a big monitor. The shelves are all covered in CD-ROMs, and then the meme says something like, We used to respect the computer. What does this mean?
Brennan: This is really giving that control element that Clay was talking about—
Beck: Mm.
Brennan: —in that we still want to honor our computer. We love computer time, right? But I think we miss that separation in which your technology wasn’t on you at all times, right? My phone is kind of just a mini computer at this point.
Beck: Yeah.
Brennan: So I think we like having some separation of, like, now it’s time for me to go in the computer room, and when I’m done, it’s done. Does that resonate with you?
Beck: Yeah. It’s a deliberate choice to go in the computer room and sit your butt in front of it and use it and then leave.
Brennan: And then leave.
Beck: I think you’re onto something. Okay, I am personally very nostalgic for Google Reader—
Brennan: Mm.
Beck: —which, for those who may not know, it was an aggregation service for websites’ RSS feeds, which doesn't sound fun, but it was.
Brennan: (Laughs.)
Beck: Um, basically, in the late 2000s, I would use this to, like, follow all my favorite blogs and cooking websites and news sources, and it was all in one place. What do you think I’m actually longing for here?
Brennan: Okay, well, I think for me what comes up here is feeling like the internet isn’t anymore curated towards what I wanna see. So for example, like I’ll open my Instagram app and I no longer see posts by my friends and family who I follow, but instead I see a lot of pushed posts. The algorithm just sends me what it thinks I wanna see. And so maybe you’re yearning for that time where the internet was curated to your niche hobbies and what you are actually interested in.
Beck: As opposed to just a bunch of slop.
Brennan: Okay, I wanna ask you one. I am also one of the analog Gen Zers who love to shoot film and collect old cameras. Thoughts?
Beck: Um, I don’t know about you, but sometimes I pick up my phone to take a picture of probably my cats, and before I know it, I’m, like, sucked into a million other things on my phone.
Brennan: Mm-hmm.
Beck: So I think, maybe, there’s also something about, like, when you wanna take a picture, you just wanna take a picture, and taking that function out of the everything device and letting it just be its own thing, maybe.
Brennan: It’s that.
Beck: Crushed it.
[Music]
Beck: Clay, I was fascinated to learn that back in the 17th to 19th century, nostalgia was considered a disease, and doctors tried to cure it with leeches. I read that there was this one American doctor who kind of thought the way to cure it was just bullying people, like shaming them with public ridicule. And, obviously, we no longer think nostalgia is literally a disease, but I think a thread of that negative attitude remains. I feel like I sometimes hear other people talk about nostalgia as though you’re trying to hide from reality, and maybe, you know, you should be a little embarrassed. Do you see that reaction from people when it comes to this current cultural yearning for a pre-digital era that, okay, it’s not a disease, but maybe it’s still not good for you?
Routledge: Yeah, definitely. People seem to have this view of nostalgia as anti-progress or holding people back from progress, and I spend a fair amount of time trying to disabuse them of that view and show them decades of empirical research. It really isn’t holding people back. We all have to adjust to change, and nostalgia helps people navigate that in the best way that they can. Even people who don’t think nostalgia’s a barrier to progress, oftentimes you see it characterized as a waste of time.
Beck: Hmm.
Routledge: Like, it’s a trivial thing, and it’s a distraction at best. Actually, nostalgia increases goal motivation. It increases a sense of meaning in life. It increases optimism. It makes people more creative. It increases empathy. Most nostalgic memories are social memories, so nostalgia actually pushes us towards each other.
Beck: When you’re saying that some people are seeing nostalgia as an impediment to progress, do you think some of that has to do with the sort of Make America Great Again brand of nostalgia where, like you’re saying, people are looking to the past to potentially bring things into the future, but sometimes what they want to bring into the future is, for instance, stricter and more stereotypical gender roles?
Routledge: So declinism is the view that things are getting worse and the past was better, whereas nostalgia really is just more of this warm feeling for the past, and I think the two are often conflated. We also find, overwhelmingly, that most of the time, nostalgia in general makes us see the humanity in other people. Or another way of saying it is: Nostalgia might be helping people wrestle with declinism—
Beck: I see.
Routledge: —and hopefully in a more productive and constructive way. A lot of Gen Z might feel like, oh, things are going in the wrong direction and their future’s gonna be worse than the future of previous generations. And there's certainly, you know, a lot of data that support that. Nostalgia’s helping them feel agentic and say, Well, you know what? We can change that. We can do something else.
Beck: It just feels surprising when you see an era that was not a great time for a lot of people recast as something to be nostalgic for.
Routledge: There are people that have nostalgia for COVID, which, again, not that long ago.
Beck: Not that fun, famously.
Routledge: Not that fun. But you know what? What’s interesting is, that wasn’t that surprising to me. When I first started doing this research, I was a professor at the University of Southampton in England. And Southampton’s a city that was heavily bombed during World War II, as a port city, and a good chunk of the city was destroyed. Not a good time. When we were doing this research, this was a little over 20 years ago, we were collecting nostalgic narratives from older British adults. Many of them were young children during that time, and they had this nostalgia.
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: But what it was is they were saying, Well, this was a time that was defining, character defining. It wasn’t a pleasant time. It shaped our character, shaped our view of the world, shaped our ability to appreciate what’s important in life.
Beck: So how does this sort of personal, individual nostalgia, right, then grow and end up becoming a cultural moment or an internet trend?
Routledge: ’Cause a lot of times what people are really looking for with nostalgia is an opportunity to share memories.
Beck: Hmm.
Routledge: Oftentimes, nostalgia is portrayed as this very isolating, personal experience. After all, this is in your head. You’re experiencing this emotion. But people love opportunities where they can talk about nostalgic experiences, particularly ones where they might have their own idiosyncratic memory of it, but it was shared with other people.
Beck: Mmm.
Routledge: I think this is why people have a nostalgia for television where you had to wait and everyone had to watch the show at the same time, and then the next day we could all talk about it.
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: You know, people are looking for ways to make contact over shared experiences where their personal nostalgia is woven into a broader cultural nostalgia that connects us.
Beck: And we’ve talked about control a good amount, and, you know, obviously we can’t actually travel back in time to an era when nobody had smartphones. Sam Altman is gonna keep making new iterations of ChatGPT, and I have no control to stop him. But do the things that we’re nostalgic for hold any lessons for how we can exert the control that we do have over the role tech plays in our lives?
Routledge: When the broader world outside of yourself, when you scale out, when it feels like you don’t have any control over that, that can be anxiety provoking; if you just focus your attention on your corner of the world, we actually do have a lot more control. Agency often happens at a local and at a personal level. You can help your neighbors. You can help your family. You can help your friends. You can be involved with those things. And even media engagement’s a way to remind ourselves of that. It’s like, Yeah, I don’t have control over the next internet iteration of a particular technology, but I can go to that retro store down the street and buy some Blu-ray discs and have a movie night at my house and have some people over.
Beck: Yeah.
Routledge: So I think people are really seeking that kind of experience.
Beck: Are you seeing people actually acting on this pre-digital nostalgia?
Routledge: There is an increased sales in physical media. The live-music market is growing. Mass attendance is up, like young people going to church.
Beck: Right.
Routledge: The number of independent bookstores and the number of chain bookstores, like Barnes & Nobles, is growing. There does seem to be something changing in our culture that’s a push back to the in-person and the analog.
Beck: Clay, I’ve noticed at many times in this conversation that you’re very optimistic about Gen Z, which is not how I often hear people talking about that generation, especially when it comes to tech. So I’m curious to hear a little bit more about how you’re thinking about it and whether Gen Z is kind of leading this trend for other generations.
Routledge: My thinking on Gen Z has really evolved, so I’m way more bullish on Gen Z—
Beck: Hmm.
Routledge: —than I used to be. So I’m a psychologist, and so when all of this research was coming out about these growing mental-health problems that young people were facing and how Gen Z reported higher rates of depression, anxiety, loneliness, pessimism for the future, like everyone else, I was like, This isn’t good.
Young people are supposed to be the ones that are optimistic. They’re supposed to be the ones that look to the future with possibility, and that didn’t seem to be the case. But then I started really studying this historical nostalgia and started seeing, like, yeah, Gen Z has their challenges, and maybe mental health is one of them, but they’re not just sitting there doing nothing about it.
They’re using their creativity and their problem-solving capacities that all humans have to do something about it, and I feel like this historical nostalgia that they’re engaging in is just one example of that. It’s not people my age that remember that time. It’s Gen Z that are saying, Hey, maybe we’re spending too much time online.
And so, for instance, there’s surveys showing that Gen Z are the generation most likely to report disconnecting from their digital devices.
Beck: Hmm.
Routledge: So now I have a different view. It’s a, you know, it’s not a certain view, of course. It’s an optimistic view, though, that Gen Z might not only be doing better than we think they are in navigating their challenges and having the agency to do so, but they actually might lead us out of this mess.
They might be the ones that remind the rest of us that there is an in-person, real-world life. So, you know, I often say that it’s common for people to feel sorry for Gen Z and worry that as digital natives, they were born too late to really appreciate the analog world.
Beck: Hmm.
Routledge: But in reality, it might be that they’re the generation that leads us back to it.
[Music]
Brennan: Mmmm …?
Beck: It sounds like you’re not so sure, Natalie.
Brennan: I said I wanted to throw my phone in the East River, and suddenly now I am tasked with healing everyone’s relationship to technology.
Beck: Not just you. Just you and your entire generation are responsible for the rest of us? Uh …
Brennan: I don’t know. I get so frustrated about this because I feel like I hear it all the time. It’s the same thing with climate change. Like, We’ll be the ones that need to fix all of it. I’m just like, This list is getting a little bit long. We’ve got a lot to fix now.
Beck: Honestly, I think what talking to Clay made me realize is that so many of us are just looking for inspiration on how to move forward with technology in a way that doesn’t feel bad. Because we have to live in 2026.
Brennan: Yeah.
Beck: It’s never gonna be 1996 again.
Brennan: Right. I think as a joint mission, then I can get behind that.
Beck: When, like, Gen Z doesn’t have to be the leader, nobody’s the leader, nobody’s the follower, we’re just figuring it out together.
Brennan: Yeah, or even bigger picture, when I feel like this is just on each one of us individually versus, you know, something that we’re all just, like, trying to renegotiate together. When it’s an individual mission, I think that’s maybe when I go escapist mode, when I go, like, fantasize about throwing the phone in the river, I wanna go back in time, back to those New England woods, to no phone.
Beck: Back to your fields, back to your compass.
Brennan: Yeah, back to my grass.
[Music]
Beck: That’s all for this episode of How to Touch Grass. This episode was hosted by me, Julie Beck, and co-hosted and produced by Natalie Brennan. Our editors are Claudine Ebeid and Jocelyn Frank. Fact-check by Gisela Salim-Peyer. Our engineer is Rob Smierciak. Rob also composed some of the music for this show. The executive producer of audio is Claudine Ebeid, and the managing editor of audio is Andrea Valdez.
Beck: Next time on How To Touch Grass:
Ashleigh Golden: A priest, a partner, a therapist, or a friend—these people have natural limits. They get tired. They push back. But the chatbot doesn't.
Elias Aboujaoude: These programs are trained to be endlessly validating and endlessly agreeable.
Beck: Turning to AI for help with anxiety could actually end up making you more anxious. That’s next time on How to Touch Grass.
articles.summary:
Gen Z is increasingly embracing analog nostalgia and pre-digital habits as a way to reclaim agency and community in an era dominated by constant smartphone and social media use.

### Key Points
- Research indicates that approximately 60% of Gen Z adults express a desire to return to a time before society was "plugged in."
- Psychologists define this trend as a self-regulatory resource that helps individuals navigate modern anxiety and uncertainty.
- Popular analog trends among younger generations include the use of digital cameras, vinyl records, physical books, and retro gaming consoles.
- Experts suggest that this behavior is not a rejection of progress, but a creative effort to balance convenience with intentional, in-person human connection.
- The podcast *How to Touch Grass*, hosted by Julie Beck and Natalie Brennan, explores these shifting relationships with technology.

### Why it Matters
This cultural shift highlights a growing desire for more meaningful, tactile experiences in a world where digital algorithms often dictate social interaction. By seeking out analog alternatives, younger generations are attempting to renegotiate their relationship with technology to prioritize personal control and genuine community.

articles.title: Exposed AWS Access Key Linked to Data Breach Affecting 1500+ UK Charities
articles.author: James Coker
articles.content:
A compromised AWS access key was the likely root cause of the cyber-attack on CRM provider Beacon, which has exposed personal information held by around 1500 UK charities.
The software provider said in an August 12 incident update that the access key was potentially exposed in public Javascript build artifacts. This suggests an error was made in the course of software development.
Beacon has assessed that the attacker used these valid credentials to access and download all data contained within the CRM platform, including attachment files, thereby impacting its entire 1500-strong customer base of charitable organizations.
This includes personal information held by charities operating in highly sensitive areas, such as healthcare and victim support.
While the data was encrypted at rest in AWS, the threat actor’s valid credentials meant its downloads would have been decrypted by AWS and available in readable form.
An analysis of Beacon’s AWS Cost & Usage reports has identified that malicious activity began on July 27, at 01:20:16 UTC and lasted for approximately one hour and 27 minutes.
This timing correlates with a significant increase in data downloads on July 27 to 28.
The CRM provider said it has not detected any attempts by the attacker to maintain persistence within its environment. It has also reset all credentials for services and accounts integrated with AWS to prevent repeat unauthorized access.
There has so far been no indication that the threat actor has published the stolen data online or otherwise misused it.
Charities Not Held Responsible for Breaches
Beacon’s charity customers have all been advised to report the breach to the UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO).
One of the confirmed victims, The Survivor’s Trust, revealed in a statement on August 13 that the ICO had already reviewed its case and concluded that the charity holds no responsibility for the breach.
The charity, which provides specialist rape and sexual abuse support services, urged its supporters to stay alert to potential scams in the coming weeks.
A number of charities have publicly declared that personal information of supporters has been compromised in recent days. These include Shrewsbury and Telford Hospital Charity, the British Deaf Association and Yorkshire's Brain Tumour Charity.
Last week, Sheffield Hospital Charity, Priscilla Bacon Hospice Charity, homelessness charity the Clock Tower Sanctuary and Victim Support, made similar public announcements.
The type of data thought to have been affected includes supporters’ names, email addresses, telephone numbers and donation records, which could provide attackers with opportunities to launch social engineering attacks on individual victims.
The compromised CRM system did not hold sensitive patient information, payment card details or bank account information.
articles.summary:
A compromised AWS access key exposed the personal data of approximately 1,500 UK charities after a security breach hit the CRM provider Beacon on July 27.

### Key Points
- Beacon confirmed that an AWS access key, inadvertently exposed in public Javascript build artifacts, allowed unauthorized access to its entire CRM platform.
- The breach occurred over an 87-minute window on July 27, resulting in the unauthorized download of all customer data and attachments.
- Affected information includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, and donation records, though no payment card or bank details were compromised.
- Beacon has reset all integrated service credentials and confirmed no evidence of persistent access or public data publication by the attacker.
- Impacted organizations include The Survivor’s Trust, the British Deaf Association, and various hospital charities, all of which have been advised to notify the ICO.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks posed by improper management of development credentials in cloud environments. For the affected charities, the breach necessitates urgent vigilance against potential social engineering attacks targeting their donors and service users.

articles.title: Chrome just flagged a hugely popular extension as unsafe
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge
articles.content:
Chrome just flagged a hugely popular extension as unsafe
Aug 13, 2026 — 12:16 PM ET
- GoFullPage, used by more than 11 million people, was pulled from the Chrome Web Store and disabled for some users.
- The extension was flagged as violating Chrome Web Store policy, triggering an “unsafe” warning.
- GoFullPage’s developer says the removal stems from a copyright issue, not a security compromise, and Google is working with the team to restore it.
Having a Chrome extension you have relied on for years suddenly red-flagged can instantly spark concerns about malware or compromised software. That exact panic hit over 11 million users this week when GoFullPage, a staple full-page screenshot utility, abruptly disappeared from the Chrome Web Store and triggered automated safety alerts across Chromium web browsers like Chrome and Brave.
Brave, for instance, is warning users that the extension may be unsafe and recommends removing it. The warning says the extension is disabled because it “violates the Web Store policy,” as shown in the screenshot below:
That understandably set off alarm bells. Several users took to Reddit after Chrome and Brave suddenly disabled the GoFullPage extension, with some wondering whether the extension had been compromised or received a malicious update. One Reddit thread shows users reporting the same warning, while another discussion on the Chrome subreddit documents the extension being disabled there, too.
But there’s an important distinction here: GoFullPage says this isn’t a malware incident.
A member of the GoFullPage team identified as Claire responded to affected users on Reddit, saying the extension was temporarily removed because of a copyright-related issue. According to the developer, Peter Coles (via Reddit), the takedown was an overreach, Google has contacted the team, and that work is underway to restore the extension. The developer also specifically denied that GoFullPage had been sold, saying that they remain at the helm.
That explanation also puts the scary “unsafe” warning into perspective. Chrome’s wording can make a policy takedown look much more sinister than it necessarily is. At this point, there’s no evidence from the reports provided that GoFullPage was compromised or distributing malware.
Still, we wouldn’t outright ignore the warning. If you rely on GoFullPage, you can wait for the developers to resolve the issue rather than downloading an unofficial copy from elsewhere. The developers claim the extension is still available on Microsoft Edge, but we couldn’t find it in the Web Store:
For now, this looks less like another compromised-extension incident and more like a minor dispute that unexpectedly knocked a very popular Chrome extension offline.
If you need a quick alternative right now, you can invoke Chrome’s built-in DevTools trick. Open DevTools (F12 or Cmd+Option+I on Mac), press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type “full”, and choose “Capture full size screenshot.” Just make sure DevTools is docked at the bottom of your screen so it captures the full layout properly. While it is not quite as seamless as clicking GoFullPage’s easy icon, it should get the job done until Google gets the official listing back online.
articles.summary:
Google has removed the popular GoFullPage extension from the Chrome Web Store after flagging the tool as unsafe, causing widespread concern among its 11 million active users.

### Key Points
- GoFullPage, a widely used screenshot utility, was abruptly disabled across Chrome and Brave browsers due to a policy violation.
- Developers confirmed the removal resulted from a copyright dispute rather than a security compromise or malware infection.
- Google is currently working with the GoFullPage team to resolve the issue and restore the extension to the Chrome Web Store.
- Users are advised to avoid unofficial versions of the software and can use Chrome’s built-in DevTools as a temporary alternative.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights how automated security warnings in web browsers can cause unnecessary alarm when policy enforcement is conflated with malware detection. It serves as a reminder for users to verify the source of software alerts before assuming a security breach has occurred.

articles.title: Armored Likho expands its cyber-espionage toolkit
articles.author: Konstantin Isakov
articles.content:
In May 2026, we discovered a new cyber-espionage campaign by the Armored Likho group, also known as Eagle Werewolf, that targets private individuals and organizations across various industries in Russia, including major corporations, the public sector, IT, and education. The attackers used a fake app as bait that mimics a service for donations. However, the most interesting part of this campaign isn’t the initial infection method – it’s the malicious implants the attackers use for cyber-espionage.
We’ve written previously about recent Armored Likho attacks, but our analysis shows that the campaign discussed below has more in common with the group’s activity from February. That said, the attackers have significantly expanded their arsenal.
During our research, we found a new cyber-espionage toolkit written in Rust: the Still Toolkit. One of its components, Still Sync, steals Telegram session data to gain ongoing access to the victim’s account. With this stolen data, attackers can leverage the Telegram API to automatically pull chat logs, media files, and other information from the account.
The second component, Still Audio, is an implant for covert audio surveillance. It analyzes the incoming audio stream, automatically detects speech, records conversations, and sends the recordings to a command-and-control server.
In this article, we’ll look at the initial infection method, how the new Still Toolkit components are built, and the technical details of how they operate.
Kaspersky products detect this threat as Trojan.Win64.Agent.* and HEUR:Backdoor.Win32.Generic.
Background
Armored Likho’s malicious activity has been documented several times before: in November 2024, and in February and July 2026. The current campaign shows significant overlap with the November and February campaigns, which used malicious droppers disguised as documents and applications related to Starlink activation or fundraising efforts as the initial infection vector. This campaign also uses fundraising as its lure. At the same time, our research uncovered a number of new tools that point to the attackers expanding their capabilities.
Initial infection
The infection chain starts with an app that mimics a donation service. As of this writing, the app distribution method remains unknown. During our research, however, we obtained several samples posing as apps from different Russian foundations.
In reality, the app is a dropper. Its developers wrote it in Rust on top of the popular Tauri framework, and it has a graphical interface designed to deceive the user. After launch, it displays a login form that asks for a password, presumably one the attackers supplied.
After the user enters a valid password, they see a catalog of donatable items. The app pulls item and category information from orderapiserver[.]info through the public/categories and public/products endpoints. A clickable catalog makes the app look legitimate. While the user browses the items, the dropper quietly decrypts and launches the payload for the next stage in the background.
Our analysis shows that the mechanism for decrypting the payload and launching subsequent stages hasn’t changed since the February campaign. However, we found a new cyber-espionage toolkit – the Still Toolkit – made up of two components: Still Sync and Still Audio.
Still Sync
Still Sync is a stealer written in Rust that steals Telegram session data. However, its capabilities don’t stop there. With this stolen data, Sync can log in to the victim’s account and pull messages and media files through the Telegram API.
Architecturally, Sync is an asynchronous application based on the Tokio library. It talks to the server over gRPC and serializes messages with FlatBuffers. It supports both HTTP and HTTPS as transport protocols; the URL of the command-and-control server determines which one it uses.
How it works
When Sync launches, the attackers set several environment variables. Before starting any malicious activity, the implant pulls configuration parameters from these:
- STILL_SYNC_ADDR: the address of the command-and-control server. By default, this is https://tg4service[.]com:443 .
- STILL_SEND_PATH: the path to the tdata
- STILL_TELEGRAM_PASSCODE: the password for decrypting the tdata folder, if Telegram data encryption is enabled on the victim’s device.
Sync also supports several command-line arguments:
- --console : runs as a console application. If this parameter is absent, the implant creates a TReload service to keep running in the background.
- --version : prints version information and exits.
- --firefly : launches a trace thread that monitors the program’s operation. It writes error messages to a hidden file, bin, located in the same folder as the main executable.
- --db : turns on debug mode with detailed logging.
Once it launches, the malware begins registering the device with the C2 server. To do this, Sync collects the following information about the victim’s system:
- Motherboard serial number
- CPU ID
- System UUID
- BIOS serial number
- Computer domain name
The malware combines the collected data into a single string with a colon as the separator. It then hashes that string with SHA-256 and stores the resulting hash under the key sysmarker. Worth noting: other Armored Likho tools, AquilaRAT included, use this same hashing algorithm.
Sync then serializes a package containing all the collected information and the agent version, and sends it in a POST request to /still.rpc.Sync/RegisterMachine. The response contains a machine_id value, which Sync uses to identify itself in subsequent requests.
Once registration succeeds, Sync sends a POST request with the machine_id parameter to /still.rpc.Sync/GetMachineSettings. The server responds with the following settings:
- enabled: triggers malicious activity on the infected device.
- scan_portable: turns on extended scanning when searching for the tdata We’ll cover this feature in more detail below.
- fetch_telegram: if this parameter is on, Sync attempts to log in to Telegram and extract data. We’ll cover this feature in more detail below.
- download_channels: if this parameter is off, Sync skips channel dialogs when exfiltrating Telegram data.
These parameters have no default values, so Sync doesn’t perform any malicious actions until the registration and settings-retrieval processes both complete successfully.
Telegram data collection
Before stealing a Telegram session, Sync searches for the tdata folder, unless the STILL_SEND_PATH variable is already set. The list of search paths includes both standard and nonstandard directories, if the scan_portable option is turned on:
- C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\: the standard Telegram Desktop installation directory.
- C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Packages\<package_folder>\LocalCache\Roaming\: the installation directory for the Microsoft Store version. Sync identifies the package folder by a name that contains the string TelegramMessenge.
- C:\: used for the extended search (if the scan_portable option is on).
Sync then sends a POST request with a list of files from the tdata folder to the /still.rpc.Sync/CheckFiles endpoint. The server responds with the following values:
- snapshot_id: an identifier the server assigns to the current data snapshot.
- present: a list of file paths that are already present on the server.
This lets the C2 server avoid re-receiving files it already has. In addition, if Sync can’t access files on disk through standard methods, it falls back on three mechanisms that abuse the SeBackupPrivilege privilege:
- Opening files with the CreateFileW function using theFILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS parameter
- Creating a backup copy through the Shadow Copy service and reading files from there
- If the previous methods all fail, attempting to copy the file using the Robocopy utility in backup mode
Beyond stealing Telegram session data, Sync can carry out full-scale collection of user information from the messaging app. When the fetch_telegram option is on, it launches a separate thread that authenticates to the chat app using the previously obtained tdata. Once authentication succeeds, Sync gains access to the account data and sends the following collected information to the server:
- User details, such as username, phone number, first and last name
- Information about private chats, groups, or channels, such as chat name and ID, the member list, and so on
- Dialogs from private chats, groups, and channels (if the download_channels option is on)
- Media files under 250MB: photos, documents, stickers, and contacts
Still Audio
Still Audio is an audio surveillance implant written in Rust. Its main job is to analyze the incoming audio stream and start recording voice when certain conditions are met – we’ll cover those in the next section. Architecturally, Still Audio largely mirrors Sync and uses the same mechanisms for communicating with the C2 server.
On launch, Still Audio performs a sequence of actions:
- It extracts libmp3lame.dll , a file stored inside the executable. This is a library used to encode audio data.
- If the --console command-line argument is absent, the implant creates a service namedauxhost , connects to it, and continues running in the background.
- While running in the background, it creates a file, logfile.log , to write logs to.
Next, Still Audio retrieves the C2 server address. As with Sync, it stores the URL in an environment variable – in this case, STILL_AUDIO_SYNC_ADDR. If that variable isn’t set, it falls back to STILL_SYNC_ADDR, which shows the two modules are compatible with each other. If neither variable is set, it uses the default URL, https://srwinservice[.]com.
Still Audio also uses the Dead Drop Resolver technique as a fallback mechanism for obtaining the C2 address. If the current server stays unreachable for three days, the tool tries to pull the current C2 URL from a GitHub repository. In the sample under analysis, we found the following URL for the page containing C2 information: hxxps://raw.githubusercontent[.]com/mmarln/pi-mono/refs/heads/main/packages/pods/src/array12.json
The repository, a fork of a popular project, contains the server URL Base64-encoded and encrypted with the Blowfish algorithm in ECB mode, using the key 5c8e153228edd3c6cbf75684 (lowercase string). Older AquilaRAT samples use this exact same algorithm and key.
Once it obtains the current C2 address, the Audio module starts a registration process similar to Sync’s, but through a different endpoint:
/still.rpc.Audio/RegisterAudioMachine. Also, unlike Sync, Audio sends a list of available audio input devices along with the system information.
The server responds with settings for the implant:
- machine_id: a unique identifier for the current device.
- vad_threshold: the threshold value for the VAD (Voice Activity Detection) algorithm. Expressed as a decimal fraction, it represents a proportion of the maximum sound level the input device can pick up. Sound above this threshold counts as voice activity. The default vad_threshold is 02.
- max_silence_duration: the number of audio samples with a VAD value below the set threshold after which the implant considers the recording finished.
- max_buffer_size: the maximum buffer size for recorded audio data.
- active_device: the name of the input device selected for recording, from the list of available devices.
The eavesdropping process
Still Audio works with raw audio samples it captures directly from the input device. To detect voice activity, it implements an algorithm based on Root Mean Square (RMS), a lightweight signal-processing method that distinguishes speech from silence by measuring the audio signal’s average power over time. The implant doesn’t rely on any third-party libraries here; it implements all the calculations itself.
The implant compares the calculated RMS value against the vad_threshold parameter. If RMS meets or exceeds this threshold, recording starts. To avoid losing the beginning of the recording, Still Audio uses a pre-buffer, a size-limited buffer that stores samples from just before the current recording moment. A sequence of max_silence_duration samples (320 by default) with RMS values below the threshold signals the end of the recording. For example, with a standard headset running at a 44.1kHz sampling rate, recording stops after roughly 7ms of silence.
Interestingly, the Audio module makes no attempt to hide its use of the microphone: its name shows up in Windows settings. In the sample we examined, the file was saved to disk as IntAudio.exe, and it appeared in the list of apps using the microphone as “Intel Audio”:
Before sending recordings to the server, the implant uses the libmp3lame library to encode the raw audio samples. It sends the recording files via a POST request to /tgfrg, adding a Client-Id header containing the machine_id obtained during registration to identify the device.
Infrastructure
This campaign draws on a broad set of hosting providers and domains registered at different points in time, which suggests the attackers are trying to make their infrastructure harder to detect. We found no direct overlap in domains or IP addresses with the February campaign. Even so, the two infrastructures share some similarities:
- They use the same hosting providers, with the ASNs 149440, 202448, and 215311.
- Their domain names follow similar naming patterns that mimic Windows system services and update mechanisms.
| Domain | IP address | Registration date | ASN | 
| orderapiserver[.]info | 187.127.153[.]38 | April 18, 2026 | 47583 | 
| tg4service[.]com | 159.198.37[.]74 | October 4, 2025 | 22612 | 
| srwinservice[.]com | 213.252.244[.]123 | March 19, 2026 | 61272 | 
| screenserv[.]com | 23.26.237[.]250 | February 13, 2026 | 149440 | 
| windowserv[.]net | 23.27.24[.]30 | February 10, 2026 | 149440 | 
| managementapiservice[.]com | 188.212.124[.]178 | May 1, 2026 | 202448 | 
| service8date[.]com | 145.223.69[.]143 | January 13, 2026 | 215311 | 
| updateservs[.]com | 145.223.68[.]66 | December 23, 2025 | 215311 | 
Victims
In this campaign, we’ve determined that the attackers’ primary targets are users in Russia. Most victims are private individuals, though the corporate sector, government organizations, IT companies, and educational institutions are also affected.
Attribution
This campaign has been using both new tools and malware families documented in BI.ZONE’s February report. While some components turned up for the first time, they show significant code-level overlap with malicious tools seen in earlier Armored Likho campaigns. Based on these overlaps, along with additional technical artifacts, we’re highly confident the Armored Likho group is behind the campaign. The overlaps we identified include:
- Identical dropper architecture in the February and current campaigns, which includes the use of the Tauri library to build the graphical interface, a similar user-input handler, a payload with the ICRYPTMP header, and the same multi-part encryption format.
- The same encryption algorithm and key used in AquilaRAT from the previous campaign and in the Still Audio module from the current campaign, both implementing the Dead Drop Resolver technique.
- Identical logic for generating the sysmarker value in older AquilaRAT samples and in the Still toolkit from the current campaign. The algorithms match down to the PowerShell commands used to collect system information.
- Substantial infrastructure overlap, which includes the hosting providers and domain-naming patterns described in the Infrastructure section.
Takeaways
The campaign described in this post shows Armored Likho’s toolkit evolving, with the group steadily expanding its cyber-espionage capabilities. Beyond the components we already knew about, the attackers rolled out new modules that let them not only access Telegram data but also conduct audio surveillance on victims. Together, these capabilities significantly widen the range of information attackers can collect in a single compromise.
One point deserves particular attention: the new tools form a cohesive set, sharing similar architecture, C2 communication mechanisms, and common implementation elements. This points to the group building out its own tool ecosystem, designed for long-term use and further expansion.
The emergence of new, specialized modules shows the attackers aren’t just trying to preserve their existing capabilities – they’re working to make intelligence-gathering more effective by controlling multiple communication channels at once.
Indicators of compromise

articles.title: Tech CEOs are writing 6,500-word manifestos. Who’s actually reading?
articles.author: Phil Wahba
articles.content:
- In today’s CEO Daily: Tech CEOs could learn from Buffett.
- The big leadership story: Traders will pay for an early look at Trump posts.
- The markets: Mixed following U.S. inflation report and Middle East tensions.
- Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune.
Good morning. Phil Wahba writing this morning from New York. Earlier this week, Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg published a few of his thoughts. Specifically 6,500 words outlining ways to spread the wealth and opportunity from AI to all people, including skeptics such as residents of communities that host data centers.
That word count made the piece about one-tenth the length of the average novel—and 10x his article on Personal Superintelligence a year ago.
And Zuckerberg is not alone: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei delivered the longest piece in this genre so far in 2024 with his 13,000-word “Machines of Loving Grace” essay, while Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has also joined in, as have other AI CEOs. The official explanation is high-minded: with Wall Street scrutinizing Meta’s tens of billions in spending and rival labs racing for dominance, these founders want to lay out their vision in exacting detail and bring regulators and the public along. As Columbia Business School professor Dan Wang told me, “They have to draw the boundaries around why AI can be useful even before they begin selling products.”
But there’s a less flattering read, and communications specialist Patrick Riccards put it best. “CEOs, particularly tech CEOs, believe that their words are gospel,” he told me. These essays, he says, are flags planted in the ground: “You essentially have five or six tech CEOs that are trying to demonstrate whose…[shall we say essay] is bigger.” In our era of short attention spans, that raises an obvious problem. Do people other than AI titans even read these? And if not, what’s the point?
For a model of what leadership via long form can actually look like, it’s useful to examine the master of the genre. Warren Buffett went long in his annual letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders—often 10,000-plus words, deep on the year’s lessons and the company’s results, sprinkled with folksy wisdom. But the length was never the point. Buffett wrote to be understood by anyone; he famously drafted his letters as if explaining the business to his own sisters, smart people who happened to be outside finance. People didn’t read him because he wrote a lot. They read him because he’d earned the right to be heard, over decades of results, and then chose to be plain about it. (His successor Greg Abel’s first letter as CEO this year followed that tradition.)
And there’s the distinction. Buffett knew exactly who his readers were. Zuckerberg, Amodei and the rest are writing to each other—a closed loop of founders, investors and the reporters who cover them, each essay answering the last. But is that the right audience? Zuckerberg is facing heat from the public, who are wary of data centers in their communities and low on trust for Big Tech. A 6,500-word manifesto seems unlikely to change their minds. If there’s one lesson any CEO can take from Buffett, it’s that the writing is easy—earning the right to be read is the hard part.

Canva lowered its expected revenue growth rate to 20% after unexpectedly high AI-delivery costs forced it to slow its rollout, despite demand for the new tools exceeding expectations. Consumer prices rose 0.1% in July and 3.4% over the past year, matching expectations, as lower energy prices offset other price pressures. KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk wrote that the "economy is a mess," warning that higher fuel costs could become more apparent in August's report.
